chunks: "Sensor fusion means combining data from several sensors to get an estimate that is better than any single one could give: more accurate, less noisy, more reliable, or with information none of them has alone.
The key idea is that sensors have complementary weaknesses. The classic example is a gyroscope and an accelerometer measuring tilt.
The gyro gives a clean, fast angular rate, and if I integrate it I get angle, but tiny bias errors accumulate, so it drifts.
The accelerometer sees gravity, so it gives an absolute tilt reference with no drift, but it is noisy and gets corrupted whenever the device actually accelerates.
So I trust the gyro in the short term and the accelerometer in the long term.
The simplest way is a complementary filter: angle equals alpha times the previous angle plus gyro rate times dt, plus one minus alpha times the accelerometer angle, with alpha around 0.
When I want to do it more rigorously, a Kalman filter treats each sensor as a measurement with a known noise variance and weights them optimally, and it can even estimate the gyro bias online.
Other examples are GPS plus IMU for navigation, where GPS fixes the slow drift of the IMU and the IMU bridges GPS dropouts, or camera plus IMU for visual-inertial odometry.
The practical details are time-stamping, calibration and handling different sample rates."
